name: AC=NC=TC
ref: Given that {thm:TC^i⊆NC^{i+1}}, and {thm:NC^i⊆SAC^i⊆AC^i⊆ACC^i&&AC^i⊆TC^i}, and NC/AC/TC are each unions of their hierarchies, these hierarchies must be equal.

name: ACC^0⊂coNQP
ref: Corollary of {thm:ACC^0⊂NQP} by taking complements, and that {lang:ACC^0} is closed under complement.

name: ACC^i⊆TC^i
ref: ACC has 'mod m' gates while TC has threshold gates. A 'w' treshold gate and a 'w+1' threshold gate let you build an 'equals w' threshold gate in constant depth. A mod m gate with n inputs can be decomposed into an OR of floor(n/m) many equality gates, so an ACC^i circuit can be mapped to a TC^i circuit with only a constant factor increase in depth and an O(n) increase in size. See for instance [here](https://cs.stackexchange.com/a/85656/11900)

name: AC^i⊆NC^{i+1}
ref: NC^{i+1} allows an additional factor of log(n) on the depth of the circuit. An unbounded fan-in OR gate from an AC^i circuit can be turned into a log(n) depth pattern of 2-fan-in OR gates to turn an AC^i circuit into NC^{i+1} at the expnese of a factor of log(n)

name: AM⊆Π2
notes: Can't find a reference for this but also not obvious to me. (Maybe it should be obvious?)

name: A_0PP⊆PP
notes: It is possible this proof is very simple and should be marked as 'obvious', I haven't looked at it yet.

name: BQP⊆QSZK
ref: Any interactive protocol with a polynomial quantum verifier also contains {lang:BQP}, by skipping the protocol entirely.

name: C_eqL⊆C_eqP
ref: Every {lang:C_eqL} machine is also a {lang:C_eqP} machine.

name: FH^1=BPP
ref: Originally stated without proof in {ref:Coo85}. The forward direction (that FH^1⊆BPP) is given by the perspective on {lang:BPP} as a reversible polynomial-size circuit with input bits, zeroed bits, and uniformly random input bits. The reverse direction is given by simulating the one layer of Hadamard gates probabilistically - which is safe because no interference or cancellation can later occur.

name: FH⊆BQP
ref: {lang:FH} is a restricted set of polynomial-size quantum circuits, those with O(1) many Hadamard layers. {lang:BQP} is all polynomial-size quantum circuits.

name: FPT⊆W[1]
ref: The W hierarchy is defined under {lang:FPT} reductions, so the class {lang:FPT} is equivalent to the trivial language in the W hierarchy -- placing it at the lowest level

name: GA⊆GI
ref: Proved in https://complexityzoo.net/Complexity_Zoo_References#kst93. Pretty simple proof but not manifest from the definition; compare with {lang:GAK} vs {lang:GIK} where the question isn't settled.

name: GIK⊆SZK
ref: Classic Graph Nonisomorphism protocol for Statistical Zero Knowledge, combined with SZK closed under complement.

name: GI⊆Δ2
ref: {lang:GI} is {lang:P} with a GraphIsomorphism oracle, while {lang:Δ2} is {lang:P} with an {lang:NP} oracle, which is at least as strong since GraphIsomorphism is in {lang:NP}.

name: IP=PSPACE
ref: Proved in {ref:Sha90}. The other direction, that {lang:IP}⊆{lang:PSPACE} and so {lang:IP}={lang:PSPACE}, from a simulation argument -- see {thm:IP⊆PSPACE}.

name: IP⊆PSPACE
ref:
This is often stated as a simple protocol simulation question, but this misses the fact that IP has private coins, and the protocol simulation approach requires public coins. See the discussion [here](https://cs.stackexchange.com/q/162804/11900). Taking the protocol simulation as the 'easy' step, this was really proved in {ref:GS86} where they showed the equivalence between private and public coins.
TODO: Technically they show that IP[f]⊆AM[f+2] for all f(n). Then since AM[f]⊆IP[f], and AM[poly]⊆PSPACE by simulation, IP=IP[poly]⊆AM[poly]⊆PSPACE.

name: LOGCFL=SAC^1
ref: Mentioned in {ref:Joh90}{ref:Ven91}, don't know where it was actually proved.
notes: Technically LOGCFL = uniform-SAC^1, and LOGCFL/poly = SAC^1. Got to make this more precise.

name: L⊆C_eqL
ref: Follows by the same construction as in {thm:P⊆C_eqP}.

name: L⊆DQC1
ref: In https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0608132 it's shown that the one clean qubit can be magnified to log(n) clean qubits without changing the class, so any computation in quantum logspace (without measurements) is in {lang:DQC1}. This includes all reversible logspace, which is equal to deterministic logspace, see Lange, McKenzie and Tapp [LMT00].

name: MA⊆StoqMA
ref: [BBT07] Sergey Bravyi, David DiVincenzo, Daniel Loss, and Barbara Terhal. The complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonian problems. Quantum Information & Computation, 8(5):361–385, 2008. arXiv:quant-ph/0606140.

name: MIPco⊆coRE
ref: A consequence of {ref:NPA08}, as they give a hierarchy that converges to the {lang:MIPco} value of a game from one above. This is contrast to {lang:MIP*}, where trying gradually larger Hilbert spaces converges from below, so it is contained in {lang:RE}.

name: NC^0⊂AC^0
ref: {lang:NC^0} circuits can only depend on constantly many input bits, so misses problems such as the OR of all inputs.

name: NC⊆P
ref: An {lang:NC} circuit is defined to only have polynomial size, and the circuit must be generated by a logspace machine, therefore a {lang:P} machine can write out the circuit and then simulate it.

name: NISZK⊆SZK
ref: By definition: non-interactive statistical zero-knowledge is a special case of statistical zero-knowledge.

name: NL⊆P
ref: There are only polynomially many states for an {lang:NL} machine, and a {lang:P} machine can enumerate all of them and check for a path.

name: NP⊆NQP
ref: {lang:NQP} can simulate any {lang:NP} machine by only using classical circuits, using Hadamard gates to prepare random ('nondeterministic') coins.

name: NQP⊆PSPACE
ref: Strong simulation of quantum circuits in PSPACE.
notes: TODO find a reference for the strong simulation.

name: Noneterministic time hierarchy theorem
notes: todo stronger statement -- currently not as tight as could be

name: ObviousConstruction
ref: Placeholder theorem for 'obvious' statements, like DTIME(f)⊆NDTIME(f), as a source for other statements. Ideally uses of this would be minimized and replaced by more precise statements that could be verified.

name: PARITY⊈AC^0
ref: {lang:PARITY} circuits, the one-language class of recognizing the parity of a string, cannot be computed by an {lang:AC^0} circuit. The same is true for any mod-m parity problem. See {ref:Raz87}{ref:Smo87}.

name: PH⊆AP
ref: {lang:PH} is polynomial time with some bounded integer k alternations, while {lang:AP} is unbounded alternations.

name: PP⊆CH
ref: The {lang:CH} hierarchy is built by taking {lang:P} and repeatedly giving {lang:PP} oracles, so {lang:PP} is the first level.

name: PZK⊆SZK
ref: By definition: perfect zero-knowledge is a special case of statistical zero-knowledge.

name: ProtocolSimulation
ref: Placeholder theorem for the general argument that a public-coin interactive protocol can be simulated by a single 'player' with sufficient time and space. To be precise, if a protocol involves r rounds of classical (resp. quantum) messages of size m between an omniscient prover and M-machine verifier, then this protocol can be simulated with `r*m` classical (resp. quantum) space, plus however much memory is needed to simulate the M-machine. This implies that all of NP, coNP, MA, AM are in PSPACE, and QCMA and QMA are in BQPSPACE (which equals PSPACE); and analogous statements, that for instance coNEXP is in EXPSPACE. It does not apply to private-coin protocols like IP, MIP, or QIP, although these often turn out to be equivalent to their public-coin variants anyway.

name: P⊆C_eqP
ref: Simple enough to be usually stated without proof, but here's the proof. Take any deterministic machine M for the language in {lang:P}. Add an initial state that nondeterministically transitions to (option A) the initial state of the original machine, or (option B) a new state that immediately rejects. This machine has one accepting path and one rejecting path if M accepts, and two rejecting paths if M rejects, so this is a valid {lang:C_eqP} machine.

name: P⊆NISZK
ref: Any interactive protocol with a polynomial verifier also contains {lang:P}, by skipping the protocol entirely.

name: P⊆PZK
ref: Any interactive protocol with a polynomial verifier also contains {lang:P}, by skipping the protocol entirely.

name: QAM⊆QIP[2]
ref: {lang:QAM} is a two-message protocol with a classical random challenge, while {lang:QIP[2]} is a two-message protocol with a quantum challenge. The latter therefore contains the former.

name: QIP[2]⊆QIP
ref: {lang:QIP} is polynomially many-rounds of quantum interactive proof, so it contains the special case of 2 rounds of quantum interactive proof.

name: QMA⊆PP
ref:
C. Marriott and J. Watrous. Quantum Arthur-Merlin Games, Computational Complexity, 14(2):122-152, 2005. doi:10.1007/s00037-005-0194-x.
 [MW05] at https://complexityzoo.net/Complexity_Zoo_References#mw05

name: QMA⊆QAM
ref: Every {lang:QMA} protocol is also a {lang:QAM} protocol, that happens to ignore the initial random challenge.

name: QSZK⊆QIP[2]
ref: Any protocol for {lang:QSZK} can be compressed to only two messages, as proved in {ref:Wat02}.

name: RBQP⊆NP
ref: {lang:RBQP} problems are {lang:NP} problems with a (quantum) efficiently calculable witness.

name: RBQP⊆RQP
ref: {lang:RQP} is, roughly the questions that can be answered by a quantum computer with zero one-sided error. {lang:RBQP} is the subset of those questions where the verification can be done with zero two-sided error by a classical computer, via a witness computable by a quantum computer with bounded two-sided error. The former can simulate the latter: try to generate a witness, and verify it with a classical circuit (which the quantum computer can run with zero error.)

name: REG⊆NC^1
ref: Given a DFA for a regular language, recursively compute the transition function induced by words of size 1, then size 2, size 4, 8, etc. until you've computed the transition function induced by the full input. Accept if that function maps the initial state to the final state. This is elaborated [here](https://cs.stackexchange.com/a/74511/11900).

name: RNC^0=NC^0
ref: An RNC^0 circuit has constant depth and bounded-fanin, therefore constant size. Therefore it has a constant number of random bits it could use, and we can just make exponentially many copies of the circuit from each random bit and take the AND of all of them. This makes it deterministic and keeps it constant size.

name: RP⊆RBQP
ref: Any {lang:RP} algorithm can be run on a quantum computer, saving the random bits, and those bits are the {lang:NP}-verifiable witness.

name: S2P⊆Σ2∩Π2
ref: The definition of {lang:S2P} includes "then there exists a z such that for all y, P(x,y,z) is false", which is a stronger requirement than if the quantifiers were swapped. Swapping the quantifiers gives the definition of {lang:Σ2}, for the first containment. Taking complements then gives the second containment.
notes: This is the trivial upper bound, see {ref:Cai01} for a better upper bound (that is a TODO to digitize: S2P⊆ZPP^NP).

name: SBP⊆A_0PP
ref: {lang:SBP} is defined in terms of {lang:#P}, and {lang:A_0PP} is defined in terms of GapP (TODO: Add). Since GapP includes all of {lang:#P} (TODO: Def), {lang:A_0PP} obviously includes all of {lang:SBP}. Alternately, see {thm:SBP⊆SBQP} as another obvious reason, and we know {thm:SBQP=A_0PP} -- TODO.

name: SZK⊆AM
ref: {lang:AM} is just {lang:SZK} where you relax the condition on not leaking knowledge

name: SZK⊆CZK
ref: By definition, all statistical zero-knowledge protocols are also computational zero-knowledge.

name: SZK⊆QSZK
ref: Classical statistical zero-knowledge is a special case of quantum statistical zero-knowledge.

name: SZK⊆coAM
ref: Taking complements of {thm:SZK⊆AM}, combined with that {lang:SZK} is closed under complement.

name: StoqMA⊆QMA
ref: [BBT07] Sergey Bravyi, David DiVincenzo, Daniel Loss, and Barbara Terhal. The complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonian problems. Quantum Information & Computation, 8(5):361–385, 2008. arXiv:quant-ph/0606140.

name: TC^i⊆NC^{i+1}
ref: NC^{i+1} allows an additional factor of log(n) on the depth of the circuit. An unbounded fan-in OR gate or THRESHOLD gate from a TC^i circuit can be turned into a log(n) depth pattern of 2-fan-in OR gates to turn an TC^i circuit into NC^{i+1} at the expnese of a factor of log(n).

name: W[P]⊆XP
ref: The W hierarchy is in terms of circuits with poly(n) inputs satisfiable by setting f(k) inputs to 1. Trying all n-choose-k inputs gives an O(n^k) algorithm to solve them, therefore all W[i] are in XP.

name: W[P]⊆para-NP
ref: The W hierarchy is in terms of circuits with poly(n) inputs satisfiable by setting f(k) inputs to 1. The set of bits to set is the witness of the {lang:para-NP} checker.

name: ZBQP⊆ZQP
ref: Follows from {thm:RBQP⊆RQP} and {thm:RBQP⊆RQP} by the definition of {lang:ZBQP} and {lang:ZQP} as their intersections.

name: ZPL=RL∩coRL
notes: the 'content' only has one way implication right now. TODO describing cocap more cleanly

name: ZPP=RP∩coRP
notes: the 'content' only has one way implication right now. TODO describing cocap more cleanly

name: ZPP⊆S2P
ref: The random seeds in a ZPP algorithm give the witnesses for the S2P protocol.
notes: This is a very weak lower bound, see {thm:Δ2⊆S2P} and {thm:MA⊆S2P} for a stronger but less obvious bound.

name: ZPP⊆ZBQP
ref: Any {lang:ZPP} algorithm can be run on a quantum computer, saving the random bits, and those bits are the {lang:NP}-verifiable witness.

name: ZPP⊆ZQP
ref: {lang:ZPP} is just the restriction of {lang:ZQP} to non-quantum circuits.

name: coNP⊆coNQP
ref: {lang:coNQP} can simulate any {lang:coNP} machine by only using classical circuits, using Hadamard gates to prepare random ('nondeterministic') coins.

name: coRBQP⊆coNP
ref: {lang:coRBQP} problems are {lang:coNP} problems with a (quantum) efficiently calculable witness.

name: coRP⊆coRBQP
ref: Any {lang:coRP} algorithm can be run on a quantum computer, saving the random bits, and those bits are the {lang:coNP}-verifiable witness.

name: nuACC^0⊆ALL
notes: Everything is contained in ALL. {lang:nuACC^0} is a nonuniform class, so it's hard to find other nontrivial containments. Any maximal nonuniform classes need to be manually marked to be in {lang:ALL}, since they won't otherwise be in the uniform hierarchies.
